look_here_first: START WITH A MATURE LEAF, not flower color. On a LOW, hairy, spreading Glandularia look for opposite leaves with SMALL BROAD, often fan-shaped major lobes (usually 3–6 pairs), sometimes subdivided, but less finely fernlike than G. bipinnatifida. Next compare the crowded terminal flowering spike and examine an OLD spike: in G. pumila its axis stays comparatively SHORT and COMPACT in fruit. Flowers are small, pale pink-purple to violet, each a single fused tube opening into five lobes. A 10× lens helps find the narrow bract below each hairy ribbed calyx. Check these characters together; either leaf size or purple flowers alone is insufficient.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Low short-lived ANNUAL, often spreading/prostrate or ascending to ~19 cm tall in Williamson County records; heights overlap other species.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Opposite decussate leaves on slender sometimes four-angled, densely hairy stems.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Mature SIMPLE leaf blade often 12–27 mm overall, broadly ovate to triangular, with 3–6 pairs of broader fanlike primary lobes and some second-order cuts.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Both ordinary stiff hairs and tiny STALKED GLANDULAR hairs, sometimes reddish-tipped, especially young shoots and flower parts.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Tight terminal flowering spike with crowded small pink/lilac-purple tubular corollas.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Corolla made of one fused tube with FIVE spreading lobes; often whitish center, NOT five separate petals.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Individual narrow bract immediately SUBTENDS each flower's hairy 5-ribbed calyx; distinguish the two only on a clearly exposed side macro.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Small compact fruiting spike whose axis does NOT elongate greatly, contrasting older elongated G. bipinnatifida spikes.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: Use mature foliage, floral tube/calyx and mature fruiting axis TOGETHER; neither flower color nor habit alone confirms species.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Small annual, commonly low/spreading or ascending, in Williamson County specimens up to ~19 cm; stems square/4-angled, often hairy with stalked glandular hairs.

key_traits.label: Leaf arrangement
key_traits.text: Opposite/decussate SIMPLE leaves, usually petiolate, at nodes on four-sided stems; pair appears at matching heights.

key_traits.label: Leaf dissected
key_traits.text: Mid-stem mature leaves often 12–27 mm, outline broadly ovate/triangular. Typically 3–6 pairs of relatively broad, fanlike major lobes with 1–2 further notches; overall less finely/regularly pinnate than most mature G. bipinnatifida. Juvenile leaves and plant vigor vary substantially.

key_traits.label: Flowering structure
key_traits.text: Short, tight terminal spike densely filled with individual flowers. One flower per narrow subtending bract; old fruiting axis grows little rather than stretching into obvious separated calyx intervals.

key_traits.label: Flower measurements
key_traits.text: Flower limb about 7–8 mm across (UT Williamson); Flower corolla tube ~4–5 mm plus throat ~2–3 mm; North Central Texas key gives corolla tube roughly 8–10 mm depending on measurement convention. Do not mix tube-only and tube-plus-throat numbers.

lookalikes.differences: G. bipinnatifida has larger, more deeply and finely 1–2-pinnately dissected leaves and generally a coarser, more feathery appearance. G. pumila is the smaller, compact, broad-lobed plant.
